children: , the global energy and liquefied-natural-gas leader, surged approximately 2.5% to $98.945 Tuesday afternoon as the global LNG market tightened sharply. Reuters reported that Asian spot LNG prices have nearly tripled to around $30 per million British thermal units, forcing price-sensitive buyers in China, India and Pakistan to lean harder on coal and oil. The squeeze is powerful for LNG suppliers, but there is a catch: prices this high can destroy the very demand producers eventually need to recover.

Shell estimates that roughly 36 million tonnes of Middle Eastern LNG supply has disappeared from the market this year. Its second-quarter results showed 18 million tonnes of LNG sales, $9.8 billion of adjusted earnings and $21.4 billion of operating cash flow, while free cash flow reached $17.5 billion. Put those numbers together and the scale becomes striking: the estimated supply loss equals two full quarters of Shell's latest LNG sales volume. For the world's largest LNG trader, disruption of that size creates both trading opportunities and unusually favorable pricing conditions.

The valuation picture says investors are already paying for part of that advantage. Shell's $98.945 share price stands 19.54% above its GuruFocus GF Value estimate of $82.77, signaling that the market currently values the company well ahead of its historical fundamentals-based benchmark. That premium raises the bar. Shell can benefit from constrained supply today, but the next leg of the story depends on whether LNG prices eventually fall enough to bring Asian buyers back without crushing the margins that made the shortage so profitable in the first place.

title: Shell Surges 2.6% as Asia's Missing LNG Demand Waits Offshore
